# Background

## Ovarian Cancer Epidemiology

The most recent "Annual Report to the Nation on the Status of Cancer"<sup>2a</sup>, published in 2025, analyzes cancer trends through 2021 or 2022, depending on data availability in the United States. According to this report, Ovarian cancer, a sex-specific cancer impacting only individuals assigned female-sex at birth, is the 11th most prevalent cancer type in U.S. females from 2017-2021 (excluding 2020), when adjusted for age-standardization among various cancer types, with an incidence of 10.4 (95% CI: 10.3-10.5) per 100,000 women<sup>2a</sup>. However, in the lagged observation period from 2018-2022, ovarian cancer was the fifth-highest cancer contributing to mortality in women (6.0 [95% CI: 6.0-6.1] per 100,000 women)<sup>2a</sup>. 

Following the all-cancer trends<sup>2b</sup>, mortality rates have steadily decreased and 5-year survival rates have steadily increased, particularly since 2005<sup>2c</sup>. Given, the discrepancy between ovarian cancer case incidence and mortality mortiality, this cancer is considered highly lethal due to it's hidden development<sup>2d</sup>. The 5-year mortality rate, based on estimates from 2016-2022, is 52%<sup>2c</sup>. However, this estimate varies drastically by stage of diagnosis. 

Stage of cancer diagnosis describe how far cancer cells have travelled from their place of origin in the body. In reference to ovarian cancer, there are 4 major staging categories, each containing various incremenatal sub-stages<sup>2e</sup>. 

**Stage I**
In stage I diagnoses, cancer cells remain in one ovary, both ovaries or the fallopian tubes. Depending on the sub-stage, cancer cells may be found on the outer surface of affected organs and/or in fluid or washings from the abdomen and pelvis.

**Stage II**
In stage II diagnoses, cancer cells originate in one- , both ovaries or the fallopian tubes, and have spread to other organs within the abdomen. Cancer cells have not yet spread to nearby lymph nodes or distant sites. 

**Stage III**
In stage III diagnoses, cancer cells originate in one- , both ovaries or the fallopian tubes, and have spread to lymph nodes and/or nearby organs outside of the pelvis. Cancer cells have not yet spread to distant sites. 

**Stage IV**
In stage IV diagnoses, cancer cells originate in one- , both ovaries or the fallopian tubes and have spread to organs or tissues outside of the peritoneal cavity, distant lymph nodes, liver and/or spleen. 

5-year survival rate for ovarian cancer diagnosed in stages I & II are estimated to be around 91.9%. Once initial diagnosis occurs in stage III, 5-year survival rates decrease to 70.1%. If cancer is diagnosted in the most advanced stages, IV, 5-year mortality rates drop to 31.5%<sup>2c</sup>. 

Unfortunately, a majority of ovarian cancer cases (54%) are diagnosed in stage IV, followed by 18% in stage III, 22% percent in stages I and II and 6% unknown staging assessments at time of diagnosis<sup>2c</sup>. 

## Current Diganosis Mechanisms

The inverse relationship between stage at diagnosis and disease prognosis, paired with high rates of late-stage diagnosis, emphasize the need for healthcare researchers and providers to assess weaknesses in the current ovarian cancer screening landscape.
